transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Markus Lee (Redwood CSM), Dana Ruiz (Velox VP Eng), Priyanka Shah (Velox SRE), Tom Brooks (Velox Security)

Summary:
Short follow-up from yesterday's escalation postmortem. Confirmed root cause (KV cache eviction + burst traffic causing model fallback loops), reviewed mitigations, and agreed on runbook + Dedicated burst pricing. Action items and owners captured.

Topics:
- Root cause recap
- Short-term mitigations (flushing, throttling, circuit breaker)
- Long-term reliability improvements (autoscaling policy, canary routing, caching strategy)
- Security/audit asks
- Next steps and owners

Action items (as discussed in call): see separate section above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, let's do a quick check-in on the Velox escalation follow-up. we want to make sure the runbook covers the KV caches and the fallback model loops.
[00:12] Dana Ruiz: Yep thanks Alex, appreciate it. We circulated the postmortem doc earlier, hope you all saw it. we're mostly focused on preventing repeat during high qps events.
[00:20] Priya Desai: I skimmed it, there was one item I wanted to highlight — the runtime's cache eviction hit an edge case when sequence lengths spiked, kv caching entries got invalidated prematurely, which pushed requests to fallback variants and created backpressure. that combined with our burst caused a compounding effect.
[00:40] Priyanka Shah: yeah from our side we saw request latencies climb then error rates spike, and we had a lot of retries from the app layer. some of the error strings were like "model unavailable" followed by redirect to smaller model, then the small model couldn't keep up.
[01:05] Tom Brooks: quick sec — security-wise we got a few SOC 2 questions in the escalation ticket about audit logs during the incident, and whether KMS access events are preserved. we need a clear artifact for the compliance team.
[01:18] Markus Lee: Markus here, I'll take point on consolidating the timeline and handing over the ElasticSearch export. I'll also coordinate with Dana on who needs the compliance artifact.
[01:26] Dana Ruiz: thanks Markus.
[01:28] Alex Kim: Cool. Priya, can you explain the kernel selection / runtime behavior that led to the eviction? you said sequence length distribution changed?
[01:37] Priya Desai: Yeah, in the report I call out that the model compilation chose a kv chunk size that was fine for median sequences but not for the 95th percentile. during the customer traffic spike we saw many requests with long context which increased memory pressure. the runtime's continuous batching gave more throughput but the cache algorithm didn't adapt quickly, so old kv entries got evicted and we paid the cost to rebuild the cache and warm up again. there's also an interplay with the quantized kernel selection where small variants had less headroom.
[02:05] Dana Ruiz: so is this more of a configuration tuning problem or a code bug in the runtime?
[02:11] Priya Desai: Mostly configuration and heuristics. we have a heuristic that decides kv shard sizes based on average seq len; when distribution shifts quickly it underestimates. we can improve heuristics and add a circuit breaker to avoid mass evictions.
[02:25] Tom Brooks: Priya, does any of this affect customer data residency or KMS keys? security needs to know if any key rotation or export happened.
[02:33] Priya Desai: No keys were rotated. the KMS calls during the incident were normal. logs show no unusual key access. but we'll produce an audit extract to be safe.
[02:45] Alex Kim: Ok good. quick question on mitigations — short-term we suggested flush+quarantine, throttle at ingress, and route to Dedicated if host capacity is near threshold. Priya, are those viable?
[02:56] Priya Desai: Yes. runbook step one: detect abnormal seq length distribution or sustained 95th percentile increase; step two: apply ingress throttling for non-critical routes and pause retries at app layer; step three: proactively flush prefix cache only for the affected model to reduce rebuild cost; step four: spin up Dedicated burst nodes or route customers to a pinned variant. the flush/quarantine is a bit tricky — you don't want to flush everything. we recommended per-customer kv flush.
[03:30] Dana Ruiz: That makes sense. the application teams are ok with per-customer flush but they want a safe, one-click runbook not to break sessions.
[03:40] Priya Desai: Understood. we'll make the runbook idempotent and include a dry-run mode.
[03:45] Mark: quick clarifying question — when you say "Dedicated burst nodes" is that a Reserved capacity or ephemeral? pricing matters.
[03:51] Alex Kim: Good point. Velox can have Dedicated burst as a short-term add-on — essentially spin up a few reserved GPUs in the customer pool with a temporary billing attachment. I'll send pricing and SLA language.
[04:05] Dana Ruiz: pricing aside, what's the expected time to spin up? during the incident it was minutes not seconds that hurt us.
[04:12] Priya Desai: Our burst orchestration can spin new containers in minutes, but full warmup to rebuild kv cache can take longer unless we pre-warm. one mitigation is to keep a small warm pool of replicas for high-risk models. that's more cost but buys recovery time.
[04:30] Tom Brooks: Sounds like we need to balance cost and RTO. Security also wants confirmation that autoscaling events are logged and that we can tie scaling actions to audit trails.
[04:40] Markus Lee: we'll add scaling action logs and an audit view to the artifact Markus will share.
[04:45] Dana Ruiz: Another ask from our SRE — can Redwood provide a health endpoint or metric that would have shown early signs of cache pressure? we didn't have anything that pointed to kv being the root cause.
[04:56] Priya Desai: Yes, we can add a KV cache hit ratio metric and expose a per-model eviction rate gauge. we already have internal metrics but we'll push those to the customer dashboard.
[05:10] Priyanka Shah: If you can push eviction rate and 95th percentile seq len we'll create a synthetic alert in our pager duty. that should catch the pattern early.
[05:18] Priya Desai: Great, we'll add both.
[05:22] Alex Kim: On the long-term side what reliability improvements did you all want?
[05:26] Dana Ruiz: We want three things: clear runbook + on-call playbook, better autoscaling heuristics that consider sequence length distribution not just RPS, and a canary routing policy to avoid full-fleet rollouts.
[05:40] Priya Desai: For autoscaling we propose a multi-signal policy: blend token-rate, active KV memory usage, and 95th percentile latency. That should reduce false negatives.
[05:50] Tom Brooks: Canary routing — is that at the model variant level? we need safe fallbacks and the ability to circuit-break to an earlier model version if quality or latency degrades.
[05:58] Priya Desai: Exactly. Canary routing at 5-10% with automatic rollback triggers if latency/errors exceed thresholds. plus a fallback policy that prefers regionally compatible variants to avoid cross-region latency spikes.
[06:12] Dana Ruiz: Okay good. can we also get a list of recommended quantization profiles? some of our smaller variants were not giving enough headroom.
[06:20] Priya Desai: We'll include suggested quantization and kernel profiles for each of your active models. we'll also add an evaluation script so you can benchmark locally.
[06:30] Alex Kim: Great. On the compliance side, Tom, is the audit artifact sufficient or do you need more?
[06:36] Tom Brooks: For now a timestamped export of KMS calls and scaling events plus the ES incident timeline should be fine. we'll review and may ask for more.
[06:45] Markus Lee: I'll bundle those together — timeline + ES export + scaling logs.
[06:50] Dana Ruiz: One more operational question — retries at our client caused extra load. do you have a recommended retry/backoff guidance?
[06:58] Priya Desai: Yes, disable aggressive retries for 5xx during degraded states and use exponential backoff with jitter. also honor 429s with Retry-After. we can provide a client-side library snippet.
[07:12] Priyanka Shah: we'll update our microservice library accordingly.
[07:16] Alex Kim: Good. Let's talk about testing — we need a validated test plan to simulate the incident and verify mitigations. Dana, do you have a maintenance window?
[07:24] Dana Ruiz: We have a nightly window next Thursday 03/18 where we can do the blast test. we'll do 10k qps sustained for 15 minutes on a staging copy of the model.
[07:34] Priya Desai: Sounds fine. we want to run the benchmark with and without the KV warm pool and capture latency and eviction metrics. we'll share an automation script.
[07:44] Alex Kim: Perfect. I'll add that to next steps. anything else on open items?
[07:50] Tom Brooks: Quick note — the legal team asked about data retention during incidents, specifically logs that may contain PII. we should include redaction guidance.
[07:59] Markus Lee: Noted. I'll coordinate with security to produce a redaction pattern.
[08:06] Dana Ruiz: Okay if no other asks, let's recap.
[08:10] Alex Kim: Recap — Priya to share full runbook and metrics for KV eviction (due 3/12), Markus to share ES timeline and scaling logs (due 3/11), Alex to send Dedicated burst pricing + SLA (due 3/15), Velox to run 10k qps test on 3/18 and upload logs. legal/compliance artifacts to be gathered by Tom/Markus.
[08:32] Priyanka Shah: Sounds good.
[08:34] Dana Ruiz: Thank you all. appreciate the quick turnaround.
[08:38] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings and truncated sentences, speaker labels mostly accurate but some overlap possible.
